extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in U.S. law, national security policy, and legal history
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and summarize the statutory prohibitions, amendments, judicial tests, and enforcement provisions described in the Wikipedia article on the Espionage Act of 1917. Covers criminal elements, postal enforcement, amendments, and key court doctrines used to interpret the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveying information to interfere with armed forces / promote enemy success
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes it a crime "To convey information with the intent to interfere with the operation or success of the armed forces of the United States or to promote its enemies' success."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishable by death or imprisonment for not more than 30 years; originally aimed at preventing interference with military operations or recruitment during wartime. Found in the core provisions of the Act (now in 18 U.S.C. ch. 37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveying false reports or statements to interfere with military or promote enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes it a crime "To convey false reports or false statements with intent to interfere with the operation or success of the military or naval forces ... or to promote the success of its enemies when the United States is at war, to cause or attempt to cause insubordination, disloyalty, mutiny, refusal of duty ... or to willfully obstruct the recruiting or enlistment service of the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishable by a maximum fine of $10,000 or imprisonment for not more than 20 years or both; targets false statements intended to disrupt military functioning or recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal enforcement and censorship authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act gave the Postmaster General authority to impound or refuse to mail publications the postmaster determined to violate its prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used historically to block distribution of publications (e.g., denial of mailing permits, impoundment) and effectively to silence certain periodicals; this administrative postal power constituted a form of prior restraint in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on transfer of combat-equipped naval vessels when U.S. neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act forbids the transfer of any naval vessel equipped for combat to any nation engaged in a conflict in which the United States is neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally uncontroversial but later complicated U.S. foreign policy (e.g., pre-WWII Lend-Lease context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition Act of 1918 amendments (speech prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments (commonly called the Sedition Act of 1918) prohibited many forms of speech, including "any disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language about the form of government of the United States ... or the flag of the United States, or the uniform of the Army or Navy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded the Espionage Act's speech-related prohibitions; these Sedition Act amendments were repealed in 1921, but cases were often brought under the Espionage Act name regardless of specific provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosure of foreign code or coded material (1933 amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1933 amendment prohibited the disclosure of foreign code or anything sent in code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted signals intelligence/code material after publication of books revealing codebreaking; reflects expansion to protect code-related secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased penalties and statutory recodification (1940, 1970, 1948 code revision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act was amended in 1940 to increase penalties and again in 1970; in the late 1940s the U.S. Code was reorganized moving much of Title 50 to Title 18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: stiffer sanctions and relocation of the statutory provisions (now in Title 18, e.g., 18 U.S.C. §794 et seq.), which affects citation and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: McCarran Internal Security Act additions and §793(e)/§798 (1950)
rubrics_metrics.description: The McCarran Internal Security Act added 18 U.S.C. §793(e) in 1950 and 18 U.S.C. §798 was added the same year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars have argued the added section potentially removes the "intent" to harm or aid requirement, possibly making "mere retention" of information a crime even without harmful intent; raised concerns about overbreadth (e.g., affecting memoirs of former officials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritorial application (1961 removal of territorial restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1961 language restricting the Act's application to territory "within the jurisdiction of the United States, on the high seas, and within the United States" was removed so the Act applies everywhere (18 U.S.C. §791).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables prosecution of conduct outside U.S. territory; prompted by specific espionage cases and concerns about applicability abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposals to broaden use of the death penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendments (e.g., 1989 by Rep. James Traficant and Sen. Arlen Specter; 1994 by Rep. Robert Dornan) sought to broaden application of the death penalty for certain Espionage Act violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects periodic legislative attempts to increase the severity of sanctions for disclosure or aiding the enemy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Act against disclosure to the press and for willful retention of classified information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act has been used not only for traditional espionage but also for prosecutions related to withholding information, communicating with members of the press, and willful retention of national defense information (e.g., prosecutions under 18 U.S.C. §793(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable cases include Pentagon Papers, prosecutions of leakers and press-related cases; enforcement trends show increasing use against media-related disclosures in recent administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial test — 'clear and present danger' (Schenck)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schenck v. United States (1919) upheld convictions under the Act but articulated the "clear and present danger" test limiting punishment to speech that presents such a danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally used to justify restrictions on speech during wartime; later jurisprudence modified the doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial test — 'bad tendency' (Abrams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abrams v. United States applied the concept of 'bad tendency' to justify restricting speech thought to have a tendency to harm governmental interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justices Holmes and Brandeis dissented, criticizing the extension of restrictions to speech without immediate danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial test — 'imminent lawless action' (Brandenburg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) changed the standard to the "imminent lawless action" test, a substantially stricter test for when inflammatory speech may be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not an Espionage Act case, this later standard influenced free-speech analysis and raised the bar for punishing speech under security statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness and 'national defense' information doctrine (Gorin and later cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have grappled with vagueness challenges to terminology like 'national defense' information and whether statutory language is sufficiently definite (e.g., Gorin v. United States and subsequent cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness arguments center on what information falls within the statute and whether ordinary citizens have fair notice; the distinction between classified material and "national defense information" is a recurring issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scienter / mens rea and 'bad faith' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law has discussed whether a defendant must act with bad faith or intent to harm (scienter) for conviction; some rulings suggest an "honest mistake" may not constitute a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have at times required proof of intent (e.g., bad faith) for certain subsections; this affects prosecution of accidental or negligent disclosures versus willful ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement discretion and geographic variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the Act's enforcement historically was left to the discretion of local U.S. Attorneys and Postmasters, leading to widely varying enforcement across locations and times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: different outcomes for the same speech in different states, political pressures shaping enforcement, and DOJ instructions requiring approval for prosecutions in some periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/operational uses of the Act beyond criminal prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act has been used administratively (e.g., to deny mailing permits, to impound materials, to restrict publication distribution) as well as criminally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative measures effectively suppressed distribution of certain periodicals and books; used by Post Office and other agencies as a form of suppression without criminal trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to foreign nationals and extraterritorial defendants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the Act against foreign citizens or acts outside the United States has been contested (e.g., cases like Zehe raising whether the Act covers foreign citizens acting abroad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have sometimes rejected extraterritorial application for purely foreign conduct; legislative changes (see 1961) and case law shape current reach.
